title: Part 4, Chapter 6
paragraphs: When he remembered the scene afterward, this is how Raskolnikov saw it.
The noise behind the door grew louder, and suddenly the door was pushed open a crack.
"What is it?" Porfiry Petrovitch cried, annoyed. "I gave orders that--"
For a moment there was no answer, but it was clear that several people stood at the door and were apparently pushing someone back.
"What is it?" Porfiry Petrovitch repeated uneasily.
"The prisoner Nikolay has been brought," someone answered.
"He's not wanted! Take him away! Let him wait! What's he doing here? This is completely irregular!" Porfiry shouted, rushing to the door.
"But he--" the same voice began, then suddenly went silent.
Two seconds, no more, were spent in actual struggle, then someone gave a violent shove, and a man, very pale, strode into the room.

The man's appearance was at first glance very strange. He stared straight ahead, as though seeing nothing. There was a look of fierce determination in his eyes, and at the same time a deathly pallor in his face, as though he were being led to the scaffold. His white lips twitched faintly.

He was dressed like a workman and was of medium height, very young, slim, with his hair cut in a round crop and thin, spare features. The man he had shoved aside followed him into the room and managed to grab him by the shoulder -- it was a guard -- but Nikolay pulled his arm free.
Several people crowded curiously into the doorway. Some of them tried to push in. All of this happened almost instantaneously.
"Go away, it's too soon! Wait till you're sent for! Why did you bring him so early?" Porfiry Petrovitch muttered, extremely annoyed, as though thrown completely off his calculations.
But Nikolay suddenly fell to his knees.
"What's this?" Porfiry cried, startled.
"I'm guilty! The sin is mine! I am the murderer," Nikolay declared, somewhat breathless but speaking fairly loudly.
For ten seconds there was silence, as though everyone had been struck dumb. Even the guard stepped back, retreated mechanically to the door, and stood there motionless.
"What did you say?" Porfiry Petrovitch cried, recovering from his momentary shock.
"I... am the murderer," Nikolay repeated after a brief pause.
"What... you... what... whom did you kill?" Porfiry Petrovitch was obviously bewildered.
Nikolay was silent again for a moment.
"Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta Ivanovna. I killed them... with an axe. Everything went dark," he added suddenly, and fell silent again.

He still knelt there. Porfiry Petrovitch stood for some moments as though deep in thought, then suddenly roused himself and waved away the uninvited spectators. They vanished instantly and closed the door. Then he looked toward Raskolnikov, who stood in the corner staring wildly at Nikolay, and started toward him, but stopped short. He looked from Nikolay to Raskolnikov and back again, and then, as though unable to restrain himself, he pounced on Nikolay.
"You're getting ahead of yourself," he shouted at him, almost angrily. "I didn't ask you what came over you. Tell me -- did you kill them?"
"I am the murderer. I want to give a statement," Nikolay pronounced.
"What did you kill them with?"
"An axe. I had it ready."
"He's in a hurry! Did you act alone?"
Nikolay did not understand the question.
"Did you do it alone?"
"Yes, alone. And Mitka is not guilty and had no part in it."
"Don't rush ahead about Mitka! How was it you both ran downstairs at that time? The porters saw you both!"
"It was to throw them off the trail... I ran after Mitka," Nikolay replied hurriedly, as though he had prepared the answer in advance.
"I knew it!" Porfiry cried in vexation. "He's not telling his own story," he muttered, as though to himself, and his eyes suddenly landed on Raskolnikov again.
He had apparently been so absorbed by Nikolay that for a moment he had forgotten Raskolnikov entirely. He caught himself, slightly taken aback.
"My dear Rodion Romanovitch, forgive me!" He rushed up to him. "This won't do. I'm afraid you'll have to leave... it's no good your being here. I will... you see, what a surprise! Goodbye!"
And taking him by the arm, he steered him toward the door.
"I suppose you didn't expect that?" said Raskolnikov, who, though he hadn't yet fully grasped the situation, had regained his nerve.
"You didn't expect it either, my friend. Look how your hand is shaking! Ha-ha!"
"You're shaking too, Porfiry Petrovitch!"
"Yes, I am. I didn't expect it."
They were already at the door. Porfiry was impatient for Raskolnikov to leave.
"And that little surprise of yours -- aren't you going to show it to me?" Raskolnikov asked sarcastically.
"Listen to him -- his teeth are chattering as he asks, ha-ha! You're quite the ironist! Well then, until we meet again!"
"I believe we can say goodbye."
"That's in God's hands," Porfiry murmured with a strained smile.

As he walked through the office, Raskolnikov noticed that many people were staring at him. Among them he spotted the two porters from the house whom he had tried to drag to the police station that night. They stood there waiting. But no sooner had he reached the stairs than he heard Porfiry Petrovitch's voice behind him. Turning around, he saw the investigator running after him, out of breath.
"One word, Rodion Romanovitch. As for the rest, it's in God's hands, but as a matter of procedure there are certain questions I'll need to ask you... so we will meet again, won't we?"
And Porfiry stood facing him with a smile.
"Won't we?" he added.
He seemed to want to say something more, but couldn't get the words out.
"You must forgive me, Porfiry Petrovitch, for what just happened... I lost my temper," Raskolnikov began. He had regained enough composure that he felt an irresistible urge to show off his coolness.

"Don't mention it, don't mention it," Porfiry replied, almost gleefully. "I have a terrible temper myself, I admit it! But we will meet again. If it's God's will, we may see a great deal of one another."
"And get to know each other inside and out?" Raskolnikov added.
"Yes, inside and out," Porfiry Petrovitch agreed, and he narrowed his eyes, studying Raskolnikov intently. "You're off to a birthday party now?"
"To a funeral."
"Of course, the funeral! Take care of yourself and get well."
"I don't know what to wish you," said Raskolnikov, who had started down the stairs but looked back again. "I'd like to wish you success, but your job is such a comical one."
"Why comical?" Porfiry had turned to go, but seemed to prick up his ears at this.

"Well, just think how you must have been tormenting and tormenting that poor Nikolay psychologically, in your usual fashion, until he confessed! Day and night you must have been hammering at him, proving he was the murderer -- and now that he has confessed, you'll start picking him apart again. 'You're lying,' you'll say. 'You're not the murderer! You can't be! This isn't your own story!' You have to admit, it's rather comical."
"Ha-ha-ha! So you noticed that I said to Nikolay just now that he wasn't telling his own story?"
"How could I have missed it!"
"Ha-ha! You're very sharp. You notice everything! You truly have a playful mind! And you always latch onto the comic angle... ha-ha! They say that was Gogol's defining trait, among the writers."
"Yes, Gogol's."
"Yes, Gogol's. I look forward to our next meeting."
"So do I."

Raskolnikov walked straight home. He was so muddled and bewildered that after arriving he sat on the sofa for a quarter of an hour, just trying to collect his thoughts. He didn't even attempt to think about Nikolay -- he was stunned. He felt that the confession was something inexplicable, something beyond his comprehension. But Nikolay's confession was an actual fact. The consequences of that fact were immediately clear: the falsehood would inevitably be discovered, and then they would come after him again. But until then, at least, he was free and had to do something for himself, because the danger was closing in.

But how close was it? His position gradually became clear. Remembering, in rough outline, the main contours of his recent scene with Porfiry, he couldn't help shuddering with horror once more. Of course, he didn't yet know all of Porfiry's aims or see through all his calculations. But he had already shown part of his hand, and nobody knew better than Raskolnikov how dangerous Porfiry's gambit had been. A little more and he might have given himself away completely, with hard evidence. Knowing his nervous temperament, seeing through him from the very first glance, Porfiry had played a bold game -- and was bound to win. Raskolnikov had undeniably compromised himself, but no actual facts had come to light yet; nothing concrete. But was he reading the situation correctly? Wasn't he mistaken? What had Porfiry been driving at? Had he really prepared some kind of surprise? What was it? Had he truly been expecting something, or hadn't he? How would they have parted if Nikolay's unexpected appearance hadn't interrupted them?

Porfiry had shown nearly all his cards -- he had taken a real risk in doing so -- and if he had truly had something up his sleeve (Raskolnikov reflected), he would have shown that too. What was this "surprise"? Was it a joke? Did it mean anything? Could it have concealed anything like a fact, an actual piece of evidence? Yesterday's visitor? What had become of him? Where was he today? If Porfiry really had evidence, it must have something to do with that man...
He sat on the sofa with his elbows on his knees and his face buried in his hands. He was still trembling with nerves. Finally he got up, took his cap, thought for a moment, and went to the door.

He had a vague sense that for today, at least, he could consider himself out of danger. He felt a sudden rush of something almost like joy; he wanted to hurry to Katerina Ivanovna's. He would be too late for the funeral, of course, but he could still make it to the memorial dinner, and there he would see Sonia.
He stood still, thought for a moment, and a suffering smile appeared briefly on his lips.
"Today! Today," he repeated to himself. "Yes, today! So it must be..."

But just as he was about to open the door, it began opening on its own. He flinched and stepped back. The door opened gently and slowly, and there suddenly appeared a figure -- yesterday's visitor from underground.

The man stood in the doorway, looked at Raskolnikov without speaking, and took a step into the room. He looked exactly the same as the day before -- the same build, the same clothes -- but his face had changed dramatically. He looked dejected and sighed deeply. If he had only raised his hand to his cheek and tilted his head to one side, he would have looked exactly like a peasant woman.
"What do you want?" Raskolnikov asked, numb with terror. The man said nothing, but suddenly bowed down almost to the ground, touching it with one finger.
"What is it?" Raskolnikov cried.
"I have sinned," the man said softly.
"How?"
"By evil thoughts."
They looked at each other.

"I was angry. When you came that day, maybe drunk, and told the porters to go to the police station and asked about the blood -- I was angry that they let you go and took you for a drunk. So angry I couldn't sleep. I remembered the address, came here yesterday, and asked for you..."
"Who came?" Raskolnikov interrupted, and instantly a memory began to stir.
"I did. I wronged you."
"So you're from that house?"
"I was standing at the gate with them... don't you remember? We've had our trade in that house for years. We cure and prepare hides, we take work home... What upset me most was--"

And the whole scene from two days earlier in the gateway came flooding back to Raskolnikov's mind. He recalled that there had been several people there besides the porters, women among them. He remembered that one voice had suggested taking him straight to the police station. He couldn't recall the speaker's face, and even now he didn't recognize it, but he remembered turning around and making some kind of reply...

So this was the explanation for yesterday's horror. The most terrifying thought was that he had nearly destroyed himself, had very nearly given everything away, over such a trivial circumstance. So this man could report nothing except his visit to the flat and his questions about the bloodstains. Porfiry, then, had nothing but delirium -- no hard facts -- nothing but this psychology that cuts both ways. So if no new facts came to light (and they must not -- they absolutely must not!), then what could they do to him? How could they convict him, even if they arrested him? And Porfiry had only just learned about the flat -- he hadn't known about it before.
"Was it you who told Porfiry... that I'd been there?" he cried, struck by a sudden idea.
"What Porfiry?"
"The head of the detective department?"
"Yes. The porters wouldn't go, so I went."
"Today?"
"I got there two minutes before you. And I heard everything -- every word of how he tormented you."
"Where? What? When?"
"Right there, in the next room. I was sitting there the entire time."
"What? So you were the surprise? But how is that possible? Good Lord!"

"I saw that the porters didn't want to do what I said," the man began. "'It's too late,' they said, 'and he might be angry we didn't come sooner.' I couldn't sleep, and I started making inquiries. Finding out where to go yesterday, I went today. The first time I went, he wasn't in. When I came back an hour later, he couldn't see me. The third time, they let me in. I told him everything, exactly as it happened, and he started jumping around the room and punching himself in the chest. 'What do you scoundrels mean by this? If I'd known about it, I'd have arrested him!' Then he ran out, called someone over, and talked to him in the corner. Then he turned back to me, scolding and questioning. He scolded me terribly, and I told him everything, including how you didn't dare say a word to me yesterday and how you didn't recognize me. He started running around again, punching himself in the chest, getting angry. And when they announced you, he told me to go into the next room. 'Sit there,' he said. 'Don't move, no matter what you hear.' And he put a chair there for me and locked me in. 'I might call you,' he said. And when Nikolay was brought in, he let me out as soon as you'd gone. 'I'll send for you again and question you further,' he said."
"And did he question Nikolay while you were there?"
"He got rid of me before speaking to Nikolay, just as he'd gotten rid of you."
The man stood still, then suddenly bowed again, touching the ground with his finger.
"Forgive me for my evil thoughts and my slander."
"May God forgive you," Raskolnikov answered.
As he said this, the man bowed once more -- not to the ground this time -- turned slowly, and left the room.
"Everything cuts both ways now," Raskolnikov repeated to himself, and he left more confident than before.
"Now we'll put up a fight," he said with a bitter smile as he descended the stairs. The bitterness was aimed at himself; with shame and contempt he recalled his cowardice.
